text.text: Holds and deposits to chase
A tour is where most venues are chosen. Show the place as it will feel on their day, answer the money questions plainly, and book the next step before they leave.
Before the tour
Inquiry details read: event type, guests, date wanted, budget
Right floor plan set up, or photos of it ready
Space clean, lights on, music low
Availability for their date and two alternatives checked
The route
Start where guests arrive: parking, entrance, coat area.
Walk the event in order: ceremony or welcome, drinks, dinner, dancing.
Show the practical places: restrooms, step-free access, caterer's kitchen, loading door.
End somewhere quiet to talk about dates and price.
Questions to ask them
What matters most about the day?
Who else is deciding, and when?
Do they have a planner or caterer in mind?
How many guests, and how firm is that number?
Answer before they ask

cells.text: Rental fee, what is included, deposit and balance dates
Approved list, or outside caterers with insurance
Access hours, end time, cleanup time
How much, and when it is returned

text.text: Closing the tour
Offer a hold: a first hold for five days if the date is free, or a second hold if someone else holds it. Set the follow-up date before they leave, and move the inquiry to
Proposal sent
once the written proposal goes out.
Virtual tours
Couples who live far away often choose from a video call. Walk the same route with a phone on a stabilizer, show the floor plan on screen, and send the same follow-up as an in-person tour.
After the tour
Send photos of the layout they liked, the proposal and the hold expiry date the same day. Note what they said mattered most on the inquiry.
Example
The Okoye-Brandt couple tours this week. They want 130 guests and an outdoor ceremony, so the terrace ceremony layout and the full-mill plan are both ready to show.
Holds and deposits are how a venue protects its calendar. Clear rules, applied the same way to everyone, avoid awkward calls.
Holds
A
first hold
lasts five working days. Before it expires, the client signs or lets it go.
A
second hold
waits behind a first. If the first lets go, call the second the same day.
Never give two first holds on the same space and date.
Enter
Hold expires
on every hold; the dashboard lists holds by expiry.
The contract

cells.text: Access from, event end, out by
Rental fee, deposit and date, balance and date
Amount, what it covers, return within 14 days
Caterer rules, insurance certificates, load-in times

text.text: Payment schedule, as a starting point
Deposit of 50 percent within 10 days of signing.
Balance 14 to 30 days before the event.
Damage deposit with the balance, returned after the post-event check.
When a payment is late
Call the client on the day after the due date, then email a summary. After 14 days, tell them in writing the date may be released. Note every call on the booking.
Balances and the event
A booking whose event date has passed but is not marked Completed shows under Overdue: usually the balance or the damage deposit has not been settled. Close it within the week.
Second holds and waiting lists
Keep the second hold's contact details and the date they asked for. Ask them if they would accept another date while they wait.
Checklist when a booking is signed
Status
Contracted
; deposit due date entered
Balance due date entered
Space and floor plan linked
Welcome email with the planning timeline and vendor rules
Example
The Adeyemi-Cooper wedding weekend is contracted for the whole mill but the deposit is not in yet; it is due in ten days, and the manager has a reminder set for the day after.

pages.title: Setup, floor plans and event day

text.text: The event day goes well when the room is set right, every vendor knows the rules, and someone owns each hour.
Two weeks before
Final walkthrough with the client or planner
Floor plan chosen and linked to the booking; table count confirmed
Caterer, rentals, florist, music: arrival and load-in times agreed
Vendor insurance certificates received; tick the box
Balance paid; damage deposit received
Floor plans

cells.text: About 10 square feet per seated guest
Leave a center aisle and clear exits
High-tops for a third of guests
Screen and power at the head

text.text: Never set more guests than the floor plan holds; the fire limit is the limit.
Setup day
Tables and chairs set to the floor plan; count against the plan.
Linens, lighting, sound checked.
Walk the exits; nothing blocks them.
Restrooms stocked; trash points set.
During the event
The venue manager is on site from vendor arrival to last vendor out.
Watch the end time, noise and occupancy.
Note anything broken, with photos, for the damage deposit check.
The run of the day
The venue manager carries the timeline: vendor arrivals, doors, dinner, speeches, last music, last guest out. Share it with the client's planner or point person and agree who calls each moment.
Teardown
Vendors out by the agreed time
Floors swept, trash out, lights off, doors locked
Damage check with photos within a day
Booking set to
Completed
; damage deposit returned or partly kept, in writing
Example
The Caldwell retirement lunch on the terrace uses the long-table plan for 48 guests. Setup is set for the day before, the caterer's arrival is being confirmed, and teardown follows straight after.
House rules protect guests, the building and the neighbors. Written plainly and shared early, they prevent arguments on the day.
Times
Access from the time in the contract; nobody sets up earlier without agreement.
Music off at 11 pm; guests out by 11:30 pm; vendors out by midnight.
Overtime is charged by the hour and must be agreed with the venue manager.
Food and drink
Caterers from the approved list, or others with insurance and a food license.
Alcohol served only by licensed bartenders; no self-service bars.
No serving to anyone under the legal drinking age or visibly drunk.
Decorations

cells.text: Nails, tape or glue on walls and beams
Battery candles; real candles in glass

text.text: Safety
Fire exits stay clear at all times.
Guest numbers never above the floor plan's limit.
Children supervised near the mill race and the pond.
First aid kit at the bar; the manager knows where the defibrillator is.
Neighbors
Guests leave quietly after 11 pm, buses wait on the drive, not on the lane, and fireworks are not allowed. Good relations with neighbors keep the license.
Damage deposit
Returned within 14 days when the venue is left as found. Deductions are listed with photos and costs. Common ones are wall marks, broken glass outside the bar area, and extra cleanup.
Sharing the rules
Send them with the contract, again with the final walkthrough notes, and to every vendor with their load-in time. Ask vendors to confirm they have read them.
Example
The art fund gala wants a fog effect for the dance floor. The manager agrees a haze machine the venue has tested, and the lighting vendor's power plan is due well before the event.

A venue sells dates, and each date can only be sold once. This workspace keeps every inquiry, hold and booking in one place, so two couples never hear yes for the same Saturday and no deposit goes unchased.
The lists

Saved layouts per space: guests, tables, setup time
Event type, guests, date wanted, how they heard about us, tour and follow-up dates, owner
Status, first or second hold, hold expiry, deposit and balance dates, rental fee, deposit, damage deposit, caterer, floor plan, setup tasks left

text.text: The booking stages
Hold
: a date is pencilled in for a few days while the client decides. A
first hold
has priority; a
second hold
moves up if the first lets go.
Contracted
: the contract is signed; the deposit is due.
Deposit paid
: the date is theirs.
Completed
: the event happened, the balance is paid, the damage deposit is returned or kept.
Your first week
Enter your spaces and the floor plans you set most often.
Add every booked date for the next 18 months with fee, deposit and balance dates.
Enter open inquiries with their next follow-up date.
Add setup tasks for events in the next three weeks.
The daily rhythm
Morning:
inquiries with a follow-up due; holds expiring this week; deposits due.
Afternoon:
tours and calls.
Before every event:
setup tasks done, floor plan set, vendor certificates in.
Example

The Hudson Valley Art Fund holds the whole mill as a first hold that expires in five days, and Corvid Labs holds the hall as a second hold. If the gala signs, Corvid's date is unaffected; if it lets go, nothing changes for Corvid either, because they want a different date.
